topic: The certification trap: why passing the exam doesn't mean you're ready for the job
post_text:
I passed my Security+ in March. Felt like I'd cracked the code to landing my first cybersecurity role.

Then reality hit during interviews.

Recruiter: "Walk me through how you'd investigate a suspicious login from an unfamiliar IP."

Me: *Blank stare. I'd memorized CIA triad definitions, not incident response workflows.*

Here's what I learned the hard way: certifications open doors. Labs open careers.

I was studying exam objectives instead of building muscle memory. No hands-on experience with SIEM tools, no exposure to real network traffic analysis, no failed investigations to learn from.

So I pivoted. Started running my own home lab—set up Splunk Community Edition, created intentional security events, practiced threat hunting for real. Built a GitHub repo documenting my findings. Took free courses on platforms like TryHackMe and HackTheBox, but this time with a focus on *application* over memorization.

Four months later, I landed a junior analyst role. The hiring manager told me it wasn't the cert—it was the lab work on my resume that made the difference.

Certifications are your ticket to the interview room. Experience is what keeps you in the seat.

If you're breaking into cybersecurity, don't skip the cert—but don't stop there either. Build something. Investigate something. Break something (in a lab).

What's holding you back from starting your first home lab? Cost? Technical knowledge? Time? I want to hear what's actually blocking you.
